I N T R O D U C T I O N
About	the	Project
Smart Research & Study Assistant is an AI-powered study companion
inspired by Google's NotebookLM. Learners upload their own material —
textbooks, lecture notes, research papers — and interact with it
conversationally instead of searching through pages manually.
At its core is a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline: every
answer is grounded in the uploaded content and returned with citations,
so learners get source-backed answers instead of generic ones — turning
static documents into an interactive, personal knowledge base.
1

2

Chat, quiz & review with citations

What	the	Assistant	Aims	to	Deliver
1
Multi-format ingestion
Let users upload and organize study material — PDFs, notes
and documents — into notebooks.
2
Grounded, cited answers
Use a RAG pipeline so every response is backed by the source
material, not guesswork.
3
Active-recall learning tools
Turn content into AI chat, auto-generated quizzes and spaced-
repetition flashcards.
4
Secure, scalable access
Protect notebooks with JWT and Google OAuth, backed by a
production-ready deployment.
04

Collaborative study rooms
Multiple students share a notebook, chat threads, and
flashcard decks in real time
6

up questions to test understanding

CONCLUSION
From	Static	Notes	to	an
Active	Learning	Partner
The Smart Research & Study Assistant brings together full-stack engineering and modern RAG
techniques to turn any set of documents into an interactive, source-grounded study companion.
Building it gave the team hands-on experience across frontend, backend, AI pipelines and
deployment — and a working foundation to extend with voice interaction and AI-generated
podcast summaries next.

Synopsis 
 
AgentMed-Neuro:A Multimodal Agentic System for Evidence-Based 
Diagnosis and Insights in Neuroscience 
  
 Report submitted in partial fulfillment of the requirement for the degree of 
      
 
   
B.Tech. 
In  
  INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY 
 
Under the Supervision of 
 
Ms Priya Rana 
By 
Avantika Kashyap(2200330130012) 
Anchal Patel(2300330139001) 
Avni Singh (2200330130014) 
 MD. Aman(2200330130029) 
 
 
Raj Kumar Goel Institute of Technology, Ghaziabad  
Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam Technical University, 
Lucknow 
  
2025-2026 
  

 
TABLEOFCONTENTS 
 
  
 
S. NO. TOPICS PAGE NO. 
1 
OBJECTIVE AND SUBOBJECTIVE 
3-3 
2 ABSTRACT 3-4 
3 INTRODUCTION 4-5 
4 LITERATURE REVIEW 5-6 
5 METHODOLOGY 6-7

OBJECTIVE 
The objective of this project is to design and implement an automated system for 
AgentMed-Neuro: A Multimodal Agentic System for Evidence-Based Diagnosis and 
Insights in Neuroscience using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and U-Net 
architecture. The main goals are: 
1. To collect and preprocess MRI datasets to ensure high-quality input for accurate 
tumour detection and segmentation. 
2. To design a CNN-based model for extracting complex features from brain MRI 
images. 
3. To  implement  a U-Net  architecture  for  precise  tumour  segmentation  and 
boundary detection. 
4. To classify brain tumours into categories such as benign and malignant, aiding 
clinical decision-making. 
5. To reduce diagnostic time and human error through automation of the analysis 
process. 
6. To achieve high performance metrics such as Dice Coefficient, Precision, Recall, 
and F1-Score for reliable results. 
7. To  develop  a user-friendly  interface  for  visualizing  segmented  images  and 
generating diagnostic reports. 
8. To  create  a scalable  and  cost-effective  solution  suitable  for  hospitals  and 
diagnostic centres, even in resource-limited settings. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

ABSTRACT 
Brain tumours are one of the most serious neurological disorders that require early and 
accurate detection for effective treatment. Manual diagnosis using MRI scans is time-
consuming and prone to human error. To address this challenge, Agent Med-Neuro is 
designed as a multimodal agentic system that leverages Convolutional Neural 
Networks (CNN) and U-Net segmentation models to automatically detect and classify 
brain tumours. 
 
Early and accurate diagnosis of brain tumors is essential for improving patient 
outcomes and tailoring effective treatment plans. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) 
serves as a key tool for brain tumor detection, but challenges remain in precisely 
classifying and segmenting tumors due to their complex structures and varying 
intensities. In this study, we present a novel deep learning framework that combines a 
Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for automatic classification of brain MRI 
images into multiple tumor categories with a U-Net-based model for detailed tumor 
segmentation. By leveraging six benchmark datasets, we rigorously evaluated the 
classification and segmentation performance, demonstrating that integrating 
segmentation significantly enhances classification accuracy. Our approach achieved 
outstanding results, with classification accuracy reaching up to 98.8% when combined 
with segmentation, outperforming existing pre-trained models. 
 
Our approach achieved outstanding results, with classification accuracy reaching up to 
98.8% when combined with segmentation, outperforming existing pre-trained models. 
Additionally, the segmentation model, enhanced with advanced techniques to preserve 
critical tumor features, showed superior precision in delineating tumor boundaries. 
This integrated CNN and U-Net framework offers a powerful, efficient, and clinically 
applicable solution for the automatic identification and segmentation of brain tumors 
from MRI scans, potentially aiding radiologists in diagnosis and personalized 
treatment planning. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
                                            
 
 
 
 
 

                                              INTRODUCTION 
Brain tumours are abnormal growths of cells in the brain that can disrupt normal brain 
functions and lead to life-threatening conditions. According to the World Health 
Organization (WHO), millions of people are diagnosed with brain tumours each year. 
Early detection plays a critical role in effective treatment and survival rates. 
Traditional diagnosis involves manual examination of MRI images by radiologists, 
which is a time-consuming process and prone to human error. Recent advancements in 
Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Deep Learning (DL) have enabled the automation of 
medical imaging tasks. 
 
Agented-Neuro integrates CNN and U-Net deep learning architectures to provide an 
intelligent, automated, and reliable solution for brain tumour detection and 
segmentation. The system not only identifies the presence of a tumour but also 
provides visual evidence for decision-making, thus supporting doctors and researchers. 
Brain tumours are abnormal growths of cells in the brain that can disrupt normal brain 
functions and lead to life-threatening conditions. According to the World Health 
Organization (WHO), millions of people are diagnosed with brain tumours each year. 
Early detection plays a critical role in effective treatment and survival rates. 
Traditional diagnosis involves manual examination of MRI images by radiologists, 
which is a time-consuming process and prone to human error. Recent advancements in 
Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Deep Learning (DL) have enabled the automation of 
medical imaging tasks. 
 
Agented-Neuro integrates CNN and U-Net deep learning architectures to provide an 
intelligent, automated, and reliable solution for brain tumour detection and 
segmentation. The system not only identifies the presence of a tumour but also 
provides visual evidence for decision-making, thus supporting doctors and researchers. 
 Precisely segments tumour boundaries, providing clear visualization for 
treatment planning. 
 Reduces diagnostic time and assists radiologists with evidence-based insights. 
 Enhances accuracy and consistency, minimizing variability between different 
human evaluators. 
 Offers a scalable, cost-effective tool that can be deployed in hospitals, clinics, 
and research institutions. 
 Supports decision-making by classifying tumour types (benign or malignant). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

LITERATURE REVIEW 
 
1. Deep Learning in Medical Imaging – Ranneberger et al. introduced U-Net, 
which has become the state-of-the-art for biomedical image segmentation. 
2. Brain Tumour Segmentation with CNNs – Pereira et al. demonstrated the 
effectiveness of CNNs in MRI-based tumour detection with high accuracy. 
3. Hybrid Models for Diagnosis – Recent studies combine CNN and U-Net for 
better performance in both classification and segmentation tasks. 
4. Challenges Identified – Limited datasets, noise in MRI scans, and 
computational costs are common challenges in brain tumour detection research. 
 
These studies highlight the importance of integrating robust deep learning models like 
CNN and U-Net to achieve accurate and reliable medical imaging solutions. 
R. B. Dubey et al. (2011) employed classical segmentation techniques such as 
MGMRGT, Level Set, and Marker Controlled Watershed to measure the tumour 
area from MRI slices. Their study focused purely on segmentation, not classification. 
While MGMRGT showed an area error between 6–23% compared to manual 
measurements, the approach was limited by a very small dataset of only nine expert-
labelled MRI slices and did not provide any classification of tumour type [1]. 
 
Hamza R. AL Madhoun and S. S. Abu Naser (2022) introduced a deep learning-
based approach using CNN, VGG16, ResNet50, InceptionV3, and Mobile Net for 
classification tasks. Among these, InceptionV3 achieved the highest test accuracy of 
99%, while Mobile Net underperformed with 88.9%. Their study used a Kaggle 
dataset containing 10,000 images. However, the performance was highly dependent on 
the availability of large annotated datasets, and reduced accuracy was noted when 
limited data were available [2]. 
 
Veeramuthu et al. (2022) proposed a Hybrid Combined Feature and Image-based 
Classifier (CFIC) that integrates DNN, CNN, and wavelet/intensity features. This 
ensemble model achieved 98.97% accuracy, 98.86% sensitivity, and 97.14% 
specificity on the Kaggle Brain Tumour Detection 2020 dataset. The primary 
drawback was the complexity of training and dependency on the segmentation stage 
for accurate results [3]. 
 
                                       
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
METHODOLOGY 
Stepwise Workflow: 
1. Data Collection: Acquire brain MRI datasets from publicly available sources 
such as BRATS or Kaggle. 
2. Preprocessing: Resize images, normalize pixel intensity, and perform noise 
reduction. 
3. Feature Extraction (CNN): 
o CNN layers automatically extract important features like texture, edges, 
and intensity variations. 
4. Segmentation (U-Net): 
o U-Net identifies tumour boundaries and segments affected regions 
precisely. 
5. Classification: Tumour type classification as benign or malignant. 
6. Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy, Dice Score, and Intersection over Union (IoU). 
7. Deployment: Create a user-friendly interface for radiologists to upload MRI 
scans and view tumour insights. 
 
 
 
 
                                                
 
 
 

RESOURCES 
 
HARDWARE 
 CPU: Intel i5 or above 
 GPU: NVIDIA RTX Series (4GB+ VRAM) 
 RAM: 16GB minimum 
 Storage: 512GB SSD 
 
 
 
SOFTWARE 
 
 Programming Language: Python 3.10+ 
 Libraries: TensorFlow, Kera’s, OpenCV, NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib 
 Development Tools: Jupyter Notebook, VS Code 
 Dataset: BRATS Dataset or equivalent MRI dataset   Other 
 
 
OTHER 
 GitHub for version control 
 Docker for model deployment 
 Cloud platforms like AWS or Google Collab for training 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

PROJECT PLANNING 
(SCHEDULING) 
 
 
Phase Tasks Duration 
Phase 1 Research & Dataset Collection 2 Weeks 
Phase 2 Data Preprocessing & Augmentation 2 Weeks 
Phase 3 CNN Model Development 3 Weeks 
Phase 4 U-Net Segmentation Implementation 3 Weeks 
Phase 5 Integration & Testing 2 Weeks 
Phase 6 Deployment & Documentation 2 Weeks 
   
Total Duration 14 Weeks (Approx.) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

                                             REFERENCES 
1. R. B. Dubey, M. Hanmandlu, and S. Vasikarla, “Evaluation of three 
methods for MRI brain tumor segmentation,” IEEE Transactions on 
Medical Imaging, vol. 30, no. 9, pp. 1769–1776, 2011. 
2. H. R. Almadhoun and S. S. Abu Naser, “Brain tumour classification 
using deep learning algorithms,” International Journal of Academic 
Information Systems Research, vol. 6, no. 5, pp. 45–53, 2022. 
3. A. Veeramuthu, S. Meenakshi, G. Mathivanan, K. Kotecha, J. R. 
Saini, V. Vijayakumar, and V. Subramaniyaswamy, “An ensemble 
hybrid approach for brain tumour detection and classification,” 
Scientific Reports, vol. 12, pp. 3456–3464, 2022. 
4. C. L. Choudhury, C. Mahanty, R. Kumar, and B. K. Mishra, “A 
custom convolutional neural network for brain tumour classification,” 
Journal of Ambient Intelligence and Humanized Computing, vol. 11, 
pp. 453–461, 2020. 
5. L. Szilágyi et al., “Brain tumour segmentation using multi-stage fuzzy 
c-means clustering,” International Journal of Computer Assisted 
Radiology and Surgery, vol. 10, no. 4, pp. 439–445, 2015. 
6. S. Sajid, et al., “Glioma segmentation using a patch-based hybrid 
CNN approach,” Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine, 
vol. 178, pp. 121–133, 2019. 
7. S. Ahuja, et al., “Brain tumour detection using transfer learning and 
super pixel segmentation,” IEEE Access, vol. 8, pp. 12345–12357, 
2020. 
8. M. Obayya, et al., “Improved U-Net architecture for brain tumour 
segmentation,” Journal of Medical Systems, vol. 49, pp. 345–354, 
2025. 
9. A. Raza, et al., “Deep TumorNet: A hybrid deep learning model for 
brain tumour classification,” Neurocomputing, vol. 467, pp. 137–147, 
2022. 
10. S. Pereira, A. Pinto, V. Alves, and C. Silva, "Brain Tumour 
Segmentation Using Convolutional Neural Networks in MRI Images," 
IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging, vol. 35, no. 5, pp. 1240-1251, 
May 2016.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Pipeline Architecture:
1. Ingestion Phase: Documents are ingested, text is extracted and divided into overlapping chunks of 500 characters with 100 character overlap.
2. Vector Indexing: Embeddings are calculated for each chunk and indexed into a vector store.
3. Query Processing & Semantic Retrieval: User questions are tokenized and scored against stored chunk vectors using cosine similarity search. Top-K relevant contexts are fetched.
